title: Joel 2:28–32
context: The LORD speaks of what will happen “afterward”: he will pour out his Spirit on all flesh, sons and daughters, old and young, even servants and handmaids (2:28–29). Wonders in heaven and earth will come before “the great and terrible day of the LORD” (2:30–31), and “whoever will call on the LORD’s name shall be saved,” with those who escape in Zion and Jerusalem, “among the remnant, those whom the LORD calls” (2:32). Versification: English 2:28–32 is Hebrew 3:1–5, and English chapter 3 is Hebrew chapter 4; this page keeps the WEB numbers. Peter cites this passage at Pentecost (see Acts 2:16–21), and Paul cites 2:32 (Romans 10:13); these notes name those uses without merging them with Joel’s own setting. On whoever will call on the LORD’s name, see the Romans 10:13 box. Shared ground: both traditions read the passage as a promise of the Spirit poured out broadly and of salvation for those who call on the LORD.

verses.text: “It will happen afterward, that I will pour out my Spirit on all flesh; and your sons and your daughters will prophesy. Your old men will dream dreams. Your young men will see visions.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD will pour out his Spirit on all flesh: sons and daughters prophesy, old men dream, young men see visions. Arminian readers see the Spirit given broadly, crossing lines of age and gender.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the promise fulfilled at Pentecost, compare Acts 2:16–17 by reference, and continuing in the church. Shared ground: both traditions read the outpouring as a gift fulfilling Moses’ wish in Numbers 11:29, named here without merging the passages.

verses.text: And also on the servants and on the handmaids in those days, I will pour out my Spirit.
verses.arminianNotes: Even servants and handmaids will receive the Spirit in those days. Arminian readers see the promise reaching the lowest social ranks, so that no one is excluded by status.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the Spirit’s work as God’s free gift, not tied to rank or merit. Both traditions read the verse as showing the breadth of the promise, which overturns the usual boundaries of who might speak for God.

verses.text: I will show wonders in the heavens and on the earth: blood, fire, and pillars of smoke.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD will show wonders in heaven and earth: blood, fire, and pillars of smoke. Arminian readers see signs accompanying God’s great acts, as in the exodus and in later judgment.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the wonders as markers of the day of the LORD, read by some as fulfilled in part and by others as still awaited. Shared ground: both traditions hold historical, typological, and future readings of these signs together.

verses.text: The sun will be turned into darkness, and the moon into blood, before the great and terrible day of the LORD comes.
verses.arminianNotes: The sun turns dark and the moon to blood before the great and terrible day of the LORD. Arminian readers see cosmic imagery announcing the seriousness of the coming day.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the language as typical prophetic description of judgment, compare Isaiah 13:10 by reference. Both traditions read the verse in more than one way, as poetic, typological, or future, and they keep these readings in conversation.

verses.text: It will happen that whoever will call on the LORD’s name shall be saved; for in Mount Zion and in Jerusalem there will be those who escape, as the LORD has said, and among the remnant, those whom the LORD calls.
verses.arminianNotes: Whoever calls on the LORD’s name will be saved, with escapees in Zion and among the remnant those whom the LORD calls. Arminian readers stress the open invitation of whoever, offered to all who call.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the pairing of calling on the LORD with being called by him, compare Acts 2:39 by reference. Shared ground: both traditions affirm that all who call will be saved.
